summary: This standards-track document lists mechanisms that keep NAT mappings alive for RTP and RTCP flows and recommends a preferred one. It is not for ICE agents, which have their own approach.

eli5.summary: A home router forgets quiet connections, which would cut a call. This lists ways to send small signals so it remembers, and picks the best.

questions: how to keep nat open for rtp
how to keep nat mapping alive for rtp
how often should rtp keepalive be sent
subtitle: Ways for RTP calls to send tiny periodic packets so a NAT does not forget the media path, and the one the RFC recommends.

tldr.problem: A NAT drops its mapping for a flow that stays quiet, and some RTP streams are quiet on purpose: one-way media, calls on hold, or very sparse text.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists six ways to send keepalive data inside the RTP session, then recommends multiplexing RTCP packets with RTP on the same address and port.
tldr.outcome: A sender must send either keepalive or media at least every Tr seconds, with 15 seconds as the minimum recommended Tr for UDP.

today: RFC 6263 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It does not apply to ICE agents, which handle NAT traversal themselves.

sections.title: Why RTP Flows Need Keepalives
sections.content:
A Network Address Translator (NAT) keeps a mapping (also called a binding) for each flow and expects it to be refreshed by traffic. Normally the RTP media packets do that on their own. This RFC covers the cases where they do not.

The text names three: a unidirectional stream negotiated with the SDP recvonly and sendonly attributes, so the receiver behind a NAT never creates a mapping; a call put on hold with sendonly or inactive, where RFC 3264 says to stop sending media and the binding may time out; and payload formats such as text conversation that send packets so rarely that the interval exceeds the NAT timeout.

The fix is for an agent to periodically send keepalive data in its outgoing RTP session, whatever the stream direction. The RFC does not apply to ICE agents, because ICE with STUN and TURN already solves NAT traversal. It also notes that a codec with its own keepalive needs nothing extra, and quotes RFC 5405: keepalives are NOT RECOMMENDED for general use.
sections.eli5: If a call goes quiet, the router may close the path, like a shop closing a door nobody walks through. A tiny periodic message keeps the door open.

sections.title: Requirements for a Keepalive Mechanism
sections.content:
The RFC sets out nine requirements, REQ-1 to REQ-9, that any mechanism should meet. Three are hard MUSTs: the mechanism must work over any transport (for example UDP or TCP), any media type (audio, video, text) and any media format (for example G.711 or H.263).

The rest are SHOULDs. Data is sent periodically for the whole stream (REQ-1). Session signaling, existing software and the remote peer should be affected as little as possible. Support should be described in SDP, and the solution should cover integration with RTCP.
sections.eli5: A good keepalive has to work for every kind of call and bother nobody, like a knock that every door understands and no neighbor minds.

sections.title: The Six Alternatives
sections.content:
The RFC lists, in no particular order, six ways to send keepalive data, each with its drawbacks.

  • Empty transport packet (4.1): send a 0-byte UDP or DCCP packet. It is specific to each transport.
  • Comfort noise RTP packet (4.2): audio only, the peer must support comfort noise and it must be signaled in SDP, and the peer may play it, so the noise level needs care.
  • RTCP multiplexed with RTP (4.3): RTCP packets sent on the same tuple as RTP. The peer must support multiplexing, some RTCP monitoring tools do not expect it, and RTCP must be configured so that Tmin is no greater than Tr.
  • STUN Binding Indication (4.4): the sender must support STUN; the RTP validity check makes the RTP stack ignore the packet.
  • RTP packet with version number zero (4.5): only four version numbers exist, so spending one is wasteful.
  • RTP packet with an unknown payload type (4.6): a 0-length packet with a dynamic payload type that was never negotiated. Its sequence number increments, its timestamp matches what media would have, its marker bit is zero and it uses the media SSRC.

The last two also depend on the peer ignoring packets it does not understand, which RFC 3550 requires but which is not always observed in real life, and some payload formats cope badly with gaps in sequence numbers.
sections.eli5: There are six ways to tap the router on the shoulder. Each has a catch, like needing the other side to understand your secret knock.

sections.title: The Recommended Mechanism
sections.content:
The RECOMMENDED mechanism is RTCP packets multiplexed with RTP (section 4.3). The RFC gives two reasons: it reduces the number of ports needed when RTP and RTCP are both used, and it takes RTCP into account, which the other mechanisms do not. All the other five are NOT RECOMMENDED.

If a media format cannot use the recommended approach, section 6 says an alternative SHOULD be defined in that format's payload format specification.
sections.eli5: The winner is to use the call's own status messages as the keepalive, so no new kind of message is needed.

sections.title: Timing and Transport Rules
sections.content:
An application MUST send either keepalive packets or media packets at least once every Tr seconds for the whole media session. For UDP the minimum RECOMMENDED Tr is 15 seconds, and Tr SHOULD be configurable to larger values. For TCP the recommended Tr is 7200 seconds.

Keepalive packets MUST use the same four-part tuple (source IP address, source port, target IP address, target port) as the regular RTP packets. An agent SHOULD send RTP keepalive only when it is not sending regular RTP packets. With the RTCP multiplexing solution, Tr MUST also follow the RTCP timing rules of RFC 3550.
sections.eli5: You must say something at least every so often, 15 seconds for the usual kind of connection, and always through the same door the call already uses.

sections.title: Keeping RTCP Itself Alive
sections.content:
RTCP is periodic, so it can keep NAT mappings open if two conditions hold. RTCP must be used bidirectionally and symmetrically as in RFC 4961, and it must be sent often enough. Some configurations break the second condition.

The RFC gives a worst-case interval formula, Twc = 1.5 / 1.21828 * members_max * rtcp_bw / avg_rtcp_size_max * 8, built from the maximum packet size, maximum number of participants and RTCP bandwidth. It also bounds the longest regular interval at 2.73123 * trr-int when bandwidth is sufficient.

Resulting rules: Twc must be no greater than Tr; with AVP or SAVP the Tmin value cannot exceed a limit derived from Tr; and with AVPF or SAVPF the minimum interval must not be set above Tr / 3.
sections.eli5: If the call's status messages come too rarely, the router forgets anyway. So the settings must make sure they come often enough.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Keepalive packets travel on the same path as regular media, so a peer could take them for an attack. The RFC points out that RFC 3550 requires a receiver to ignore packets with payload types it does not understand, so a peer that does not understand the keepalive will correctly drop it.
sections.eli5: A keepalive might look odd to the other side, but a polite receiver simply ignores anything it does not understand.
